title: Aula del Simonino
clean:
Above the door of this house, a painted inscription still says that a blessed child was born here. It's a lie, and it has been kept there on purpose.

You're on Via del Simonino, in the old centre of Trento. Look at the front of the building: the fifteenth-century windows uncovered in the restoration, and the eighteenth-century figures and lettering painted back in. The room behind it was, until recently, known as the Chapel of the Simonino.

Here's what happened. In Easter week of fourteen seventy-five, a little boy called Simon, about two years old, went missing, and was found dead in a ditch beside a house belonging to a Jewish family. The Prince-Bishop of Trento, Johannes Hinderbach, backed the accusation that the town's small Jewish community had killed him in a ritual murder. It was the old blood libel, and it had no truth in it at all.

Jewish men were arrested and tortured for months. In June that year they were executed. The women were put on trial after them. The community was expelled from Trento, and Jews did not return to live in the city until nineteen ninety-two. Even at the time, a papal envoy spoke out against the accusation.

[beat]

And yet the child became a cult. Simon was venerated as a martyr for almost five hundred years, with processions, relics and chapels like this one. It wasn't until nineteen sixty-five that the cult was finally suppressed, the processions stopped, and his remains were taken away.

In twenty eighteen the house was given away by Marina Larcher Fogazzaro, so that it could be opened to the public. Rather than tidy the story away, the room has been turned into a place to tell it. Inside, you listen on headphones to a sound piece of about twenty minutes, narrated by the actress Daria Deflorian.

When you leave, walk to Piazza Duomo. Since January twenty twenty-five there's been a plaque there remembering the Jews of Trento who were tortured and killed in fourteen seventy-five. It's worth standing in front of both.

notes: The child's name, age and discovery date differ between FAI (Simone Lomferdorm, a little over two, found 24 March) and Wikipedia (Simon Unverdorben, about two and a half, missing 23 March). The script says 'Simon, about two years old' and 'Easter week'.
1965: FAI says papal decree; Wikipedia says Archbishop Gottardi. The script says 'the cult was finally suppressed' without naming who.
The 1992 return of Jews to Trento is FAI's claim.
The plaque in Piazza Duomo (27 January 2025) is from Wikipedia.
Eighteen men arrested (Wikipedia); the script says 'Jewish men' without a number.
